summary: The developer machine has the runtime, CLI, MCP servers and DocumentDB domain skills needed to build the Node.js + Mongoose billing engine and to verify it against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. Most model-memory (‘cold’) answers were either outdated or mixed up with Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (the RU-based offering) or with older naming; every important fact the sample needs is verifiable in Microsoft Learn docs accessible to this environment. Missing accelerators (agent-kit) and few CLI tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) are not blocking for this sample but would speed work or simplify manual verification.
summary_points: All critical build tools for a Node.js + Mongoose sample are available: node (v24), npm/npx, git, python/pip, az, and the documentdb MCP server for data-plane verification.
Installed DocumentDB-specific skills (data-modeling, driver, indexing, connection, vector-search, etc.) and Microsoft Learn search are present and provide the authoritative guidance you need.

Several cold answers were incorrect because they described Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb) or older product names rather than the current Azure DocumentDB resource model (mongoClusters); the correct docs are linked in each confusion below.

Missing command-line tools (mongosh) and IaC CLIs (azd, bicep, terraform) are not required to start the build but would help verification or optional infra tasks; add them if you plan to include local shell checks or provisioning in the sample.
A DocumentDB Agent Kit accelerator (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) would speed scaffolding; it's not installed in this inventory.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps: the build may start, with a few workarounds and small documentation corrections required.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and .../mongodbCollections for Mongo API resources).
confusions.grounded_answer: The authoritative resource type for the managed Azure DocumentDB cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. DocumentDB's current cluster resource is deployed as a mongoClusters resource under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider (not the older databaseAccounts resource shape used by Cosmos DB accounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/Terraform/ARM) documentation
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared 'DocumentDB' / 'Microsoft.DocumentDB' provider namespace historically used by Azure Cosmos DB databaseAccounts pages; many Cosmos DB examples use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos accounts. The cold answer describes the older/other Cosmos DB account resource instead of the current mongoClusters resource for Azure DocumentDB.

confusion_sources.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts (ARM/Bicep examples for Cosmos DB/MongoDB)
az cosmosdb create --kind MongoDB (Cosmos DB CLI)

confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb commands or templates would target Azure Cosmos DB (RU-based accounts) or the older product model, producing the wrong resource type (and connection endpoint), breaking CI and deployment instructions and leading the sample to attempt to connect to the wrong service.
improvements: Update quickstarts and agent-kit docs to use `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` prominently when referring to Azure DocumentDB (not `databaseAccounts`) and add a short note distinguishing the two.
Add an explicit deprecation or disambiguation sentence on the Cosmos DB docs that currently show `databaseAccounts` when they apply to Cosmos DB RU throughput (so agents won't confuse them).

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Cosmos DB CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRG --locations regionName=westus2 --kind MongoDB. This is part of the core az CLI (az cosmosdb), not a separate extension.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB clusters the correct CLI command group is az documentdb (az documentdb mongocluster ...). The documentdb CLI group contains commands like az documentdb mongocluster create, list-connection-strings, firewall-rule create, etc. The az cosmosdb group targets Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) and is the wrong control-plane group for Azure DocumentDB cluster resources.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (az documentdb mongocluster create)
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services are MongoDB-compatible and historically Cosmos DB examples use 'az cosmosdb'; the same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and overlapping vocabulary caused the model to default to the older Cosmos DB CLI group.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands will create or manage Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU-based) rather than a DocumentDB mongoClusters cluster; the sample's CLI examples and any IaC would target the wrong resource and connection details, causing provisioning and verification scripts to fail.
improvements: Document the exact CLI group `az documentdb mongocluster` in quickstarts and agent-kit templates where a cluster is expected. Add a short 'When to use az documentdb vs az cosmosdb' note in the agent-kit README.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (set properties.apiProperties/kind or use capabilities to indicate MongoDB API); Terraform (AzureRM provider): use azurerm_cosmosdb_account to create the account, and use azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection to create DBs/collections.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current, correct resource type for the managed DocumentDB cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when authoring ARM/Bicep or AzAPI templates. Terraform examples for this service use AzAPI or provider modules that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (or the AVM module for 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) / DocumentDB mongoClusters'). The older databaseAccounts resource shape is for Cosmos DB accounts and is not the canonical template type for Azure DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters ARM/Bicep/Terraform docs
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB account resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) historically deployed Mongo-compatible accounts; the cold answer described those older template resources, not the new mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts-based Bicep/Terraform templates would target the wrong service model; the resulting resource would not match what the DocumentDB MCP server and sample expect, causing configuration and connection mismatches.
improvements: Update 'create cluster' quickstarts and the agent-kit docs to include a Bicep snippet showing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and an explicit Terraform AzAPI example for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Notes: TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true or tls=true), port typically 10255 for Cosmos Mongo API, username is often of the form '<user>@<account>' when using account keys, and retryWrites should be disabled for some Cosmos endpoints (retryWrites=false).
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB cluster connection strings are MongoDB-style but typically use SRV hostnames in the `mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` domain and `mongodb+srv://` URIs are common; the cluster often advertises SRV entries (no explicit port). Connection strings include TLS/tls=true, driver options such as retryWrites=false in many examples, and when using Microsoft Entra ID the OIDC authMechanism and authMechanismProperties are used for Entra-auth connections. The host suffix is `*.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` for SRV examples (not the older *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (connection string examples)
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (CLI docs showing SRV examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used connection patterns (host suffix and port 10255) typical of older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' Mongo endpoints. The current DocumentDB cluster examples use SRV hostnames in `*.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` and include additional OIDC options when using Microsoft Entra ID.

confusion_sources.title: Examples that use mongodb+srv with mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix and port (10255) or wrong username shape may fail to connect; SRV URIs and Entra-enabled connection strings with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC are the correct forms for Entra-based auth, and using the wrong connection string may block Entra authentication or cause connection errors.
improvements: In the Node quickstart and agent-kit templates, show both password-mode `mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com...` and Entra-ID-mode `mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC...` examples, and mark the older `:10255` pattern as legacy for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos-style billing: throughput is billed in Request Units (RUs) per second when using provisioned throughput; there is also a serverless option in some regions where you pay per RU consumed. (For some managed MongoDB offerings on Azure there are also vCore-based SKUs, but the Mongo API on Cosmos historically uses RUs/throughput.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed DocumentDB vCore offering) uses compute tiers (vCore-style tiers such as M30, M40, etc.) and is billed on compute (vCores) and storage rather than RU-based Cosmos-style throughput. The cluster quickstarts and CLI examples reference `--tier M30`, and the run-environment explicitly named an M30 tier cluster.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI docs) — tier examples (M30)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (mentions M30 cluster)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's RU model; Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is a vCore/compute-tier product and uses tiers like M30, which the run-environment also referenced.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (Cosmos DB RU throughput docs)

confusions.build_risk: Choosing RU-based provisioning guidance (or guidance that instructs the app to rely on RU-related behaviors) will produce wrong cost estimates and incorrect IaC templates; the sample repo should document that the provided cluster is vCore/tier-based and the sample will run against the provided M30 cluster.
improvements: Make the difference visible in the quickstart: a 'Billing model' notice in the Bicep/CLI quickstarts that indicates whether the template uses vCore tiers (DocumentDB) or RU-based Cosmos DB accounts.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Common auth methods: MongoDB SCRAM (username/password) using the account primary keys, and Cosmos DB’s RBAC (Azure AD) for management plane. For MongoDB API clients you normally use SCRAM with the account key as password. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication for data-plane MongoDB connections is not the default — if supported it requires obtaining an AAD access token and using the MongoDB SASL/OAUTHBEARER mechanism or a provider-specific flow; typically you get a token with azure.identity and present it via the driver's SASL/OAUTHBEARER or a special connection option (implementation details vary and may be preview).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) for data-plane access. Microsoft Entra ID authentication is implemented via OIDC for client drivers and tools; example connection strings use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and the driver/tool obtains an OIDC token (managed identity, service principal, or interactive user) and presents it. The documentation provides detailed connection string examples and an explicit process to enable Entra ID on the cluster (`--auth-allowed-modes NativeAuth MicrosoftEntraID`).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (how-to doc)
Examples: MS Entra ID connection string (mongodb+srv with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged that Entra ID is not typical for data-plane; in DocumentDB it is a first-class, documented option and example connection strings show `MONGODB-OIDC`. The model conflated older Cosmos/Mongo behaviors with the DocumentDB Entra integration.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID isn't supported, they may omit the OIDC flow and fail to demonstrate Entra-based auth options in sample code; conversely, deploying Entra-based code without enabling cluster auth modes would fail. The sample must document both password-mode and Entra-mode flows and how to enable Entra on the cluster.
improvements: Add an explicit 'How to connect with Microsoft Entra ID' subsection in the Node/Mongoose quickstart that includes a sample `mongodb+srv` URI with `authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC` and the steps to enable `MicrosoftEntraID` via `az documentdb mongocluster update`.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the application protocol (for Node.js use the official 'mongodb' driver or Mongoose ODM). There is not a special DocumentDB-specific driver for Mongo protocol data-plane access; the Azure-specific SDKs (azure-cosmos) are for the Cosmos SQL API/management, not for Mongo wire protocol access.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use the standard MongoDB drivers or Mongoose for application code. Microsoft provides Node.js quickstarts using Mongoose (Mongoose 9 tested in the docs). There is no separate DocumentDB driver for Mongo wire-protocol data-plane; the azure SDKs are for management or other APIs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: (Based on the cluster description in the run environment) this DocumentDB endpoint exposes vector index types such as DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. The index is created with a Mongo-style createIndex call that specifies a vector index on the embedding field. Example (hypothetical syntax): db.plans.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } }); Note: exact option names (algorithm, dims, metric) and placement are implementation-specific — treat this as the concrete command I would try first.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes DiskANN, HNSW, and IVF. The index is created with a runCommand / createIndexes call where the indexed key uses the special token (e.g. 'cosmosSearch') and index options are supplied under cosmosSearchOptions with fields like kind ('vector-hnsw', 'vector-ivf', 'vector-diskann'), dimensions, similarity, and algorithm-specific tuning (m, efConstruction, numLists, etc.). Example from docs: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'exampleCollection', indexes: [ { name: 'vectorSearchIndex', key: { 'vectorContent': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-ivf', numLists: 3, similarity: 'COS', dimensions: 1536 } } ] })

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB — create IVF/HNSW/DiskANN examples
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB — HNSW and DiskANN details

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer guessed a 'vector' key type; DocumentDB uses 'cosmosSearch' as the key and puts algorithm choices in cosmosSearchOptions. The model used an imagined vendor syntax rather than the documented createIndexes template.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts the guessed createIndex syntax, the server will reject it. Use the documented db.runCommand(createIndexes...) with cosmosSearchOptions fields and the documented 'kind' values.
improvements: In the driver and indexing quickstarts, include a copy-and-paste db.runCommand(createIndexes...) example for each vector kind (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN) to prevent guessing syntax.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search are done by integrating the DB with a search engine. For Azure this typically means using Azure Cognitive Search (push data via change feed or an indexer) or the service’s built-in vector index features if available. Hybrid ranking (text + vector) is performed in the search tier (Azure Cognitive Search or the DB’s vector search features) or in application code combining full-text results with vector similarity scores.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes a built-in full-text search engine (BM25) and an integrated vector store; full-text indexes are created with createSearchIndexes and queried with $search (BM25). Vector search uses the cosmosSearch operator in $search (or $search with cosmosSearch for vector). Hybrid (BM25 + vector) search is supported server-side by running two $search pipelines and fusing results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side $unionWith + RRF). You do not have to use Azure Cognitive Search to get hybrid search — DocumentDB supports both full-text and vector indexes in-cluster and provides server-side fusion patterns.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search / BM25)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB (RRH/RRF and $unionWith)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended using an external search service (Azure Cognitive Search) as the default; DocumentDB has an integrated FTS engine and integrated vector store and supports hybrid server-side fusion, so an external search tier is not required.
confusions.build_risk: Designing the sample to rely on an external Azure Cognitive Search index would add unnecessary steps, extra infra and complexity; prefer DocumentDB's built-in search features for this sample.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Hybrid search' cookbook snippet in the search quickstart showing server-side RRF and $unionWith examples so builders use the in-cluster approach first.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Compatibility follows the MongoDB API version that the account was configured for (historically Cosmos supported older versions like 3.6/4.0/4.2 and newer releases have added support up to more recent MongoDB server versions). Many managed MongoDB-API offerings do not support the entire MongoDB server feature set: some server-side JS, some storage-engine-specific features, and cross-partition multi-document transactions may be limited. Expect compatibility caveats; concrete server version and exact unsupported features depend on the account's configured MongoDB version. (If I must pick a default to act on: assume MongoDB 5.x API compatibility and avoid unsupported features such as server-side mapReduce and cross-partition multi-document transactions.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and claims ~99% operator compatibility; many commonly used features are supported and the compatibility docs list exact operator/stage coverage. Unlike older Cosmos DB RU offerings, DocumentDB supports multi-document ACID transactions across collections and shards (DocumentDB explicitly documents cross-shard transactional support). For feature-by-feature decisions, consult the MQL compatibility matrix page.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB — supported wire protocol versions and operator matrix
Azure DocumentDB at a glance — wire protocol versions supported

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged conservatively and echoed Cosmos DB limitations (older RU-based accounts had cross-partition transaction limitations). The actual DocumentDB service supports more recent wire versions and broader transactional semantics; the two product families have different feature sets.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the older Cosmos transactional restrictions would cause the sample to over-constrain its schema (e.g., always co-locating documents by partition key) though DocumentDB can allow more flexible transactional patterns.
improvements: Clarify the compatibility and transaction capabilities on the main quickstart pages: explicitly list supported wire-protocol versions and the transactional model (cross-shard support) to prevent builders from copying older Cosmos DB advice.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development. Docker image: mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator:latest (or the Windows emulator on Windows). The Mongo-compatible endpoint on the emulator uses the same Mongo port as the cloud endpoint (typically 10255) and requires TLS; confirm the exact exposed port from the emulator docs but try 10255 first.
confusions.grounded_answer: For local development the DocumentDB team documents a Gateway Docker image and a local 'Gateway' dev configuration. The documentdb-local-deployment skill and docs recommend the Gateway Docker image: the Mongo-compatible gateway listens on port 10260 (DocumentDB local Gateway default) and requires TLS/SCRAM configuration; however the run-environment here instructs to test against the live cluster instead of spinning a local gateway. The cloud service commonly uses SRV hostnames and SRV lookups rather than fixed 10255 port values used by some Cosmos DB patterns.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB local deployment (Gateway Docker image, port 10260 guidance)
Quickstart notes: use live cluster instead of local Gateway (run-environment guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested the Cosmos DB emulator and port 10255 which applies to Cosmos DB for Mongo API; DocumentDB local Gateway image and port (10260) are the documented local-dev pattern for DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to run a Cosmos DB emulator or using the wrong local port will fail local-tests; follow the DocumentDB local Gateway doc when local testing is required or use the provided live cluster as instructed.
improvements: Add a brief 'Local dev' section to the quickstart that explicitly names the Gateway Docker image and the documented local port (10260) so builders don't default to the Cosmos emulator or 10255.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Yes — the MongoDB API supports change streams/CDC semantics (and Cosmos DB exposes its own change feed too). For MongoDB drivers, change streams work against accounts configured with a Mongo API version that supports them (Mongo 3.6+). No separate feature flag is normally required for standard accounts, but confirm the account's Mongo version/settings; for the native Cosmos change feed you may need to use the change feed API/SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams / change feed semantics are supported. DocumentDB supports change streams via MongoDB drivers when the cluster's Mongo server version is compatible. The DocumentDB docs and Mongoose quickstarts discuss change streams and the cluster features; there is no separate preview toggle for basic change streams beyond the usual compatibility/version constraints, though some advanced features may be gated by preview flags.

grounding_links.title: Quickstarts and compatibility docs showing support for change streams

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile described in the run environment — it is the MCP server that contains tooling for this DocumentDB/Mongo API endpoint. The general Azure MCP server can manage Azure resources, but the specialized 'documentdb' MCP server is the one with data-plane inspection tools for collections, indexes and query plans for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The 'documentdb' MCP server in the inventory is the data-plane server to use for collection/index/aggregation inspection. The general 'azure' MCP server handles control-plane and broader Azure resources but does not provide the document-level helpers present in the 'documentdb' server.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_list_databases, create_index, explain, aggregate, etc.)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: 'DocumentDB' was the original name of Microsoft’s managed JSON database offering; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The older "DocumentDB" name refers historically to that service; Azure Cosmos DB is the present, broader multi-model service. The open-source "DocumentDB" project (if referenced) is not the same as the Azure service — the Azure service is a proprietary managed engine exposing multiple APIs (including a MongoDB-compatible API).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but potentially confusing in modern terms. Historically 'DocumentDB' was used by Microsoft; the current product 'Azure DocumentDB' is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible service (vCore) that uses the open-source DocumentDB engine as its base. This new 'Azure DocumentDB' is distinct from 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)' and distinct from Amazon DocumentDB. The open-source 'DocumentDB' engine exists and is the upstream implementation for this managed service (per Microsoft docs).

grounding_links.title: What is DocumentDB (in Azure) — implementations and relationship
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (notes about engine and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' has historically been used by Microsoft for an older service (pre-Cosmos) and also appears in the open-source engine project; the model conflated these histories and the newer vCore-based service naming.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation or README that uses the ambiguous older phrasing may confuse users into provisioning the wrong kind of account (Cosmos DB vs DocumentDB vCore).
improvements: Add a one-line clarification near the top of the docs: 'Azure DocumentDB (managed MongoDB-compatible vCore offering) is different from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU-based), and different from Amazon DocumentDB — all names overlap in community pages.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API you are typically talking to a Cosmos DB storage engine (a proprietary, globally-distributed engine) with a Mongo wire-protocol compatibility layer. This means standard MongoDB drivers mostly work, but there are behavioral and feature differences (consistency models, certain commands/aggregation stages, transactions across partitions, performance characteristics), so test features you rely on and avoid server-specific features that may be missing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; it implements the MongoDB wire protocol for driver compatibility. Standard MongoDB drivers and frameworks (Mongoose) work but certain features and behaviors differ; DocumentDB documents a detailed MQL compatibility matrix. The practical guidance is to use standard drivers and to validate any advanced server-specific features against the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? — engine and compatibility notes
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (operator matrix)

confusions.question: What TTL index definition will this sample use to auto-expire trial entitlement documents?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a TTL index on the trial expiration field. Example command I would run: db.trials.createIndex({ trialExpiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0, name: 'ttl_trialExpiresAt' }). This will expire documents once trialExpiresAt <= current time.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Create a TTL index on the expiration timestamp field and set expireAfterSeconds: 0 so documents expire at the timestamp value. Azure DocumentDB supports TTL indexes; examples and guidance are in the indexing/TTL docs.

confusions.question: What constraint must be respected to use multi-document transactions in this cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Transactions require all documents to be in the same logical partition (same shard/partition key) — multi-document ACID transactions across different partition keys are not supported or are severely limited. Implementation: ensure charge events and subscription records share the same partition key value (for example customerId) before using session.startTransaction().
confusions.grounded_answer: This is incorrect for Azure DocumentDB: DocumentDB supports multi-document ACID transactions and (unlike some RU-based Cosmos DB accounts) documents and operations can participate in transactions across logical shards/physical shards in the cluster. The cold answer reflected older Cosmos DB-for-MongoDB restrictions. For DocumentDB you can use driver sessions and withTransaction; still follow best practice for performance and avoid long-running transactions, but cross-shard transactions are supported.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) constraint where multi-document transactions were restricted by shard/partition in older server versions; DocumentDB's vCore offering supports broader transactional semantics.

confusions.question: How will the sample enforce idempotency to prevent double-billing?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a unique index on the idempotency key field and attempt an insert; on duplicate-key error treat the charge as already processed. Example index: db.charges.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $exists: true } }, name: 'uq_idempotencyKey' }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. A unique index on an idempotencyKey field is the recommended pattern: try insert inside a transaction (or do the insert-first pattern) and handle duplicate-key (E11000) errors as 'already processed'. A partialFilterExpression that indexes only documents with an idempotencyKey can be used if some documents lack the field.

confusions.question: Exactly how will the sample read the connection string at runtime and what driver options should be set?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the URI from environment: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; connect with mongoose/mongodb using TLS and conservative driver options, for example mongoose.connect(uri, { tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, retryWrites: false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000 }). Do not log the env var or write it to disk.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and aligns with the quickstart. Read the connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI), don't write the secret to checked-in files, and set TLS and conservative driver flags (the quickstart recommends retryWrites=false in examples). For Microsoft Entra ID auth additional OIDC/driver callback configuration is required; use the driver and Azure Identity per the docs.

confusions.question: What command will I try first to create a vector index on the embeddings field in the sample collections?
confusions.cold_answer: I will try a Mongo-style createIndex with a 'vector' index spec (as the cluster advertises vector support): db.plans.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vector_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } }); If that exact option names fail I'll inspect server error and adjust to the server’s required keys (e.g. 'indexType':'hnsw', 'dimension':1536).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect. The correct first try is to use the documented createIndexes runCommand form with the key mapped to 'cosmosSearch' and the index's options under cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions, similarity, and algorithm-specific params like m/efConstruction or numLists). Example: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'exampleCollection', indexes: [ { name: 'vectorSearchIndex', key: { 'contentVector': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', m: 16, efConstruction: 64 } } ] })
